newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks look ready to plumb new depths.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks look ready to plumb new depths.

text.p: Japanese stocks appear ready to plumb new depths in the coming months amid a crisis of confidence in the government's ability to shore up the economy and worries over health of the country's financial sector.

Analysts said the benchmark Nikkei share average is on the verge of falling through 18,000, fuelling fears that such a decline would spark further "triple weakening" in Japan's assets -- the yen, stocks, and government bonds.
Such selloffs, dubbed by traders as the "selling of Japan," would be inevitable if stocks continue to decline, they said.
The Nikkei took another steep tumble on Wednesday, falling 1.14 percent to its lowest close in more than a year to 18,680.38, on deepening gloom about the economy.

Casting a long shadow over the market was a lack of confidence in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's ability to help sustain the nation's economic growth while carrying out much-needed structural reforms, traders said.
"The government has not felt it urgent to hammer out a new plan just by the Nikkei 225's break through 19,000," said Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
"It will be necessary for it to hit around 18,000 to prompt the government to change its policy," he said.
The market is focussing on the economic details of Hashimoto's policy speech before parliament on January 20, but traders said expectations were already low.
"There is a possibility that the government will not do anything and let financial firms close their books (for the fiscal year) in the red. Then the Nikkei may dive to around 17,000," Mabuchi said.
The Nikkei, however, could swing back to 20,000 if Hashimoto proposes an extra budget to reinforce the economic recovery or a drastic change in land taxes, he said.

Yasunari Ueno, chief economist at Fuji Securities Co Ltd, said few options were left for the government. "It would be difficult for the government to propose something effective (on January 20)," Ueno said.
He said Tokyo cannot craft a huge increase in spending for the economy at the same as it musters up a tightening of the budget amid mounting fiscal debts.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka already sounded an alarm on Wednesday, saying that big firms must take the lead in boosting the economy and not rely too much on the government.

Also undermining the market are renewed concerns that financial firms, already burdened with hefty bad loans, will be unable to handle losses caused by the stock plunge, which trim latent profits from their share holdings.
Shares in the financial sector have been depressed recently by lingering worries over banks' bad loan problems.

Akira Takai, a senior analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research Institute Ltd, estimated unrealised stock profits held by the top 20 banks totalled 9.85 trillion yen as of Wednesday, down 36 percent from the end of September 1996.
The profits would disappear for most of the banks if the key Nikkei average fell further to about 14,900, he added.
Takai said that, although he did not think falling stocks alone would directly hinder the banks' plans to write off their bad loans, the decline would weaken their financial health.
"If the stock decline rekindles major banking worries here by weakening the banks' financial health, we might see a vicious circle," Takai said. "That's our biggest concern."
Traders said the sharp stock falls may drive financial firms into selling shares or bonds to eke out profits before closing their financial books in March.
